production.waterSource: Yamazaki was selected for its high-quality local water at the confluence area of the Katsura, Uji and Kizu rivers; Suntory identifies the area's water and humid microclimate as fundamental to the distillery.
production.fermentation: Suntory deliberately uses different washback types and yeast regimes to create multiple component-spirit styles. Exact washback counts and fermentation durations are not admitted because current first-party public sources emphasise diversity rather than one fixed specification.
production.stills: Yamazaki uses multiple differently shaped copper pot stills rather than a single uniform still design, enabling production of a broad range of malt component spirits. Suntory confirms direct firing is used for first distillation as part of its quality approach, alongside continuing pilot-distillery research into alternative heating technologies.
production.maturation: A wide range of cask types is deliberately used to create diverse malt components suitable for long-term maturation. The humid Yamazaki climate is treated by Suntory as an important part of maturation conditions.

profiles.houseCharacter: Yamazaki is designed around diversity rather than one narrowly fixed new-make style. Different washbacks, pot-still geometries, direct-fired first distillation and varied cask types allow Suntory to produce many distinct malt components at one physical site. Those components are built to withstand long ageing, with Yamazaki's humid climate and broad cask repertoire adding further differentiation during maturation.
profiles.cask23Narrative: Yamazaki is best understood as a whisky-making laboratory at full distillery scale. Instead of relying on one still shape or one fermentation regime, Suntory deliberately creates multiple styles of new make using different washbacks, still geometries and cask types, then brings those components together through maturation and blending expertise. That production diversity is one of the reasons Yamazaki can show such breadth while remaining recognisably rooted in the same historic Japanese distillery.

production.malt: The Balvenie retains traditional floor maltings and grows part of its own barley. Established specialist technical references state that only a minority of total malt demand is produced on site, with the balance purchased externally.
production.fermentation: Established specialist references describe approximately 65-hour fermentation in large washbacks, producing a sweet, malty wash.
production.stills: The distillery operates multiple wash and spirit stills with tall necks and reflux features. Specialist references describe five wash stills and six spirit stills, with distinctive reflux balls and differing lyne-arm orientations that promote separation and a sweet, refined spirit.
production.peat: The standard house style is essentially unpeated; once a year The Balvenie produces a separate smoky spirit during its Peat Week programme using peat prepared through its own malting operation.
production.maturation: The distillery maintains an on-site cooperage and is strongly associated with American-oak whisky casks, European-oak sherry casks and secondary cask finishing, a technique pioneered at The Balvenie by David C. Stewart.

profiles.houseCharacter: Balvenie's production architecture is built around preserving sweetness while maintaining texture. Floor-malted barley contributes a traditional cereal base, while long fermentation and high-reflux still geometry favour honeyed, fruity spirit with relatively little roughness. Its extensive in-house cooperage and finishing programme then layers vanilla, spice, dried fruit and other cask-derived notes onto that sweet Speyside core.
profiles.cask23Narrative: The Balvenie is unusual not because one single production feature dominates, but because so many traditional crafts remain on site. Floor malting, resident coppersmithing and cooperage feed into a spirit designed to be naturally honeyed and supple. That makes it especially responsive to the distillery's famous use of secondary cask maturation and wood finishing.

production.waterSource: Benriach draws mineral-rich water from an underground aquifer beneath the distillery grounds and uses a distinctive four-water mash.
production.malt: Benriach produces both unpeated and Highland-peated spirit and periodically revives its own floor maltings during its annual Malting Season.
production.fermentation: The official site links the sweet four-water mash to a fruit-forward wash; established specialist technical references describe eight washbacks and an unusually long fermentation averaging around 100 hours.
production.stills: Benriach operates four main copper pot stills, two wash and two spirit stills, and distils deliberately slowly. The distillery also makes small annual runs of triple-distilled spirit.
production.peat: Benriach distils a Highland-peated style as well as its classic unpeated spirit, using mainland peat to create a sweeter woodland-smoke profile rather than a medicinal coastal peat profile.
production.maturation: Benriach uses an unusually broad cask palette sourced globally, including bourbon, sherry, wine and other fortified-wine casks, with stocks held in both traditional dunnage and larger warehouse formats.

profiles.houseCharacter: Benriach deliberately builds fruit before the spirit reaches the cask: its mineral-rich water, four-water mash and long fermentation favour ester formation and orchard-fruit character. Slow distillation then preserves a broad heart cut, while the distillery can switch among unpeated, peated and occasional triple-distilled styles. That flexible spirit architecture is designed to work with an unusually diverse cask inventory rather than one narrowly defined maturation regime.
profiles.cask23Narrative: Benriach is best understood as a Speyside distillery built for flavour diversity. Its long, sweet fermentation and slow distillation create a fruit-forward core, but the same site also produces Highland-peated and occasional triple-distilled spirit. That gives the maturation team an unusually wide canvas, which is why Benriach expressions can range from orchard-fruit Speyside elegance to sweet smoke and richly cask-driven styles.

production.waterSource: The Dalmore identifies Loch Morie as its water source.
production.fermentation: The 2026 distillery expansion added Oregon-pine washbacks. No precise fermentation-duration figure is admitted because it is not published in the verified first-party source set.
production.stills: The Dalmore's asymmetric copper stillhouse is intentionally preserved through exact Forsyths replicas. The stills use boil balls to increase copper contact; wash stills have distinctive flat-topped heads with side outlets into long winding lyne arms, while spirit stills use water jackets around the heads and necks to promote reflux.
production.maturation: The distillery operates a multi-cask maturation philosophy supported by long-standing relationships with major bodegas and wineries, using cask selection as a central part of the house style.

profiles.houseCharacter: The Dalmore's robust, fruity new make is shaped by an intentionally asymmetric set of stills rather than a uniform stillhouse design. Boil balls, unusual wash-still vapour paths and water-jacketed spirit stills create different levels of copper contact and reflux, producing complementary spirit weights. That structurally complex new make is designed to withstand long and layered maturation across sherry, wine and other high-impact cask types.
profiles.cask23Narrative: The Dalmore's production story begins with unusually individual still geometry rather than a standardised set of identical pots. Different still shapes create distinct spirit personalities, with added reflux and copper contact refining the new make while retaining weight. That strong, fruity base is then deliberately built for sophisticated multi-cask maturation, which is why wood management is so central to The Dalmore's identity.

production.waterSource: Soft Highland water is drawn from springs associated with the Dronac Burn on the distillery grounds.
production.malt: Scottish malted barley is used; small volumes of peated spirit have also been produced.
production.fermentation: Traditional Scottish larch washbacks are used. Established specialist reporting places fermentation at roughly 55-60 hours for the current robust, weighty style.
production.stills: The distillery uses four copper pot stills, two wash and two spirit stills, with the distinctive saxophone-shaped geometry highlighted by the distillery.
production.peat: The house style is primarily unpeated, with limited peated production occurring separately.
production.maturation: Pedro Ximénez and Oloroso sherry casks are central to the house style, with maturation in traditional dunnage warehouses.

profiles.houseCharacter: A relatively compact fermentation regime and robust Highland new make preserve cereal weight and dark-fruit potential rather than chasing maximum lightness. The saxophone-shaped stills retain body while still allowing enough copper contact for fruit and texture to remain articulate. Long maturation in Oloroso and Pedro Ximénez casks then amplifies dried fruit, nut, spice and natural colour into the deeply sherried style for which GlenDronach is known.
profiles.cask23Narrative: The GlenDronach is built around a substantial Highland spirit designed to stand up to long maturation in richly seasoned sherry oak. Traditional larch washbacks and distinctive saxophone-shaped stills help preserve weight and texture before the whisky moves into Oloroso and Pedro Ximénez casks in dunnage warehouses. For customers, that means the sherry influence is not simply a finish laid over a delicate spirit; it is integrated with a muscular new make capable of carrying deep dried-fruit, nut and spice character for decades.

production.waterSource: The distillery uses pure water from the Lake District National Park in whisky production.
production.malt: Unpeated malted barley is used for The Lakes single malt.
production.fermentation: Three different yeast strains are combined to build layered flavour. Fermentation is extended to as much as 96 hours, deliberately reaching malolactic fermentation to increase complexity and creamy texture.
production.stills: The distillery uses copper pot distillation with separate wash and spirit stills. Distillation is run slowly to maximise copper contact and retain a robust, fruity spirit suited to active maturation.
production.maturation: The house philosophy is explicitly sherry-led and wood-forward. The distillery has expanded racked warehousing on site to support maturation and stock growth.

profiles.houseCharacter: The Lakes begins with unpeated malt and intentionally long, multi-yeast fermentation to create a robust, fruity and textural wash. Slow copper-pot distillation maximises copper contact while preserving enough body for active wood influence. The resulting spirit is engineered specifically for a sherry-led, wood-forward maturation regime rather than for neutral cask treatment.
profiles.cask23Narrative: The Lakes Distillery designs its spirit with maturation already in mind. Three yeast strains and fermentation of up to 96 hours build fruit and texture before slow copper distillation creates a spirit strong enough to stand up to assertive sherry-led wood. It is a useful example of modern English whisky making where fermentation, distillation and cask design are treated as one connected flavour system.

profiles.location: The Macallan Estate, Easter Elchies, Craigellachie, Moray

production.waterSource: The current distillery continues to use the same estate water source and raw-material regime as the previous Macallan site; established technical sources describe on-site spring water in production.
production.fermentation: The current distillery uses stainless-steel fermenters fitted with external cooling to control temperature within the integrated stillhouse/tun-room environment. Exact current fermentation duration is not disclosed in the verified source set.
production.stills: The current distillery contains 36 small copper pot stills arranged in three circular pods: 12 wash stills and 24 spirit stills. Macallan deliberately retains unusually small spirit stills to maximise copper contact and preserve its rich, fruity distillate style.
production.maturation: Macallan operates a highly controlled oak programme centred on sherry-seasoned European and American oak alongside ex-bourbon casks, with wood sourcing, seasoning and cooperage specification managed as a core part of production.

profiles.houseCharacter: Macallan's unusually small spirit stills create high copper contact while retaining enough weight to produce a rich, fruity new make. The modern distillery uses temperature-controlled stainless fermentation to reproduce the established spirit character despite a radically different building. Its highly managed sherry-seasoned oak programme then provides much of the dried-fruit, spice and polished oak character associated with mature Macallan.
profiles.cask23Narrative: The Macallan's modern distillery looks radically different from the old site, but the production brief was continuity rather than reinvention. Its signature remains the use of unusually small spirit stills and a tightly controlled oak programme, especially sherry-seasoned casks. For the drinker, the key idea is that the distillery engineers a rich fruit-driven spirit first, then uses carefully specified wood to build depth rather than relying on cask influence alone.

production.waterSource: Established specialist sources identify Gearr Abhainn as the distillery water source.
production.malt: The same physical distillery makes unpeated Tobermory and heavily peated Ledaig spirit. Specialist technical references describe Tobermory malt at very low phenol levels and Ledaig at roughly 35 ppm or higher.
production.fermentation: Four wooden washbacks are used. Established specialist sources report variable fermentation, approximately 50-100 hours, with longer runs supporting fruit development.
production.stills: Two wash stills and two spirit stills are used. The stills incorporate reflux bowls and distinctive S-shaped/kinked lyne arms, increasing reflux; shell-and-tube condensers are used.
production.peat: Peat is a deliberate production split: Tobermory is the unpeated house spirit, while Ledaig is the heavily peated style from the same distillery.
production.maturation: Only limited warehousing is retained on site; a significant proportion of maturation takes place away from the distillery, while special or limited stocks can be held locally.

profiles.houseCharacter: Tobermory's unusual still geometry creates meaningful reflux despite the distillery's relatively oily spirit texture. Variable fermentation length allows fruit character to develop before the spirit reaches the two pairs of stills. The same hardware then supports two distinct malt streams—unpeated Tobermory and heavily peated Ledaig—making malt specification rather than separate plant one of the key determinants of style.
profiles.cask23Narrative: Tobermory is really two whisky personalities made in one historic Isle of Mull distillery. Unpeated Tobermory and smoky Ledaig share the same fermentation and distinctive kinked-lyne-arm stillhouse, so the major stylistic split begins with the malt itself. That makes the site a useful example of how a single set of hardware can produce dramatically different whiskies when peat specification is changed deliberately.

profiles.owner: Tomatin Distillery Co. Ltd. (Takara Shuzo group)

production.waterSource: Tomatin uses naturally soft water from the Alt-na-Frith burn.
production.malt: Scottish malted barley is used. The core Tomatin spirit is unpeated; a lightly peated production run made for roughly one week each year is used for Cu Bocan.
production.fermentation: Twelve stainless-steel washbacks are documented by established specialist sources. Published specialist fermentation figures conflict materially, so no exact duration is admitted to the governed profile.
production.stills: Twelve tall, slim copper pot stills remain installed at Tomatin, arranged as six wash and six spirit stills, although production utilisation varies. The tall still geometry supports the distillery's light, soft and fruity spirit style.
production.peat: Tomatin's core spirit is unpeated; the distillery separately produces a lightly peated spirit for Cu Bocan during a limited annual production period.
production.maturation: Official material emphasises a broad wood policy including bourbon, sherry, refill and wine/fortified-wine casks, with both dunnage and racked warehousing represented in established technical sources.

profiles.houseCharacter: Tomatin combines soft Highland water with tall, slim stills to produce a light and fruit-forward new make rather than a heavy spirit. The site retains unusually large installed still capacity, but production is managed for quality rather than the scale that once made Tomatin Scotland's largest malt distillery. A broad wood policy then gives the gentle spirit enough flexibility to support both classic bourbon/sherry maturation and more experimental cask programmes.
profiles.cask23Narrative: Tomatin's modern identity is almost the opposite of its historic reputation for sheer scale. Although twelve stills remain on site, the distillery now emphasises a softer, fruitier spirit made with Alt-na-Frith water and tall copper stills, then develops that spirit through a broad cask programme. The separate lightly peated Cu Bocan run shows how the same plant can also create a different house stream without redefining the core Tomatin style.

profiles.location: Sleat Peninsula, Isle of Skye, Scotland

production.malt: Scottish two-row spring barley is used, with malt dried over peat smoke for the core house style.
production.fermentation: Traditional Douglas-fir washbacks are used. An established Skye technical source reports eight wooden washbacks and fermentation varying approximately 70-120 hours; the distillery's own published material confirms that fermentation length is an actively controlled flavour variable.
production.stills: Torabhaig uses twin Forsyths copper pot stills designed specifically for the restored steading: one wash still and one spirit still.
production.peat: Peat is central to the distillery's 'smoke with taste' house style, but the exact PPM level varies across production and is not hard-coded here as a single facility-wide number.
production.maturation: The majority of new make is filled to first-fill bourbon casks sourced from Kentucky, with sherry and virgin-oak components used for selected releases.

profiles.houseCharacter: Torabhaig builds its spirit around peated malt, long flavour-driven fermentation and a compact two-still plant rather than high-volume production. The distillery treats fermentation length, yeast, cut points and peat level as active variables, which is why its smoky house style is expressed with significant fruit and textural variation. Bourbon-led maturation preserves that smoky-fruity core while selected sherry and virgin-oak casks add additional structure.
profiles.cask23Narrative: Torabhaig's aim is not simply to make heavily smoky whisky, but to make peat carry flavour. Its Douglas-fir washbacks, twin Forsyths stills and variable fermentation programme are used to build fruit and texture underneath the smoke, while first-fill bourbon remains the main maturation foundation. That is the production logic behind the distillery's own phrase 'smoke with taste'.

production.waterSource: Tullibardine uses water from the Danny Burn, fed by mineral-rich springs in the Ochil Hills.
production.fermentation: The current official site states the distillery has 10 washbacks; established specialist sources describe stainless-steel washbacks and a minimum fermentation of roughly 52 hours.
production.stills: Four copper pot stills are operated on site: two wash stills and two spirit stills. Established specialist sources report wash-still capacities around 21,500 litres and spirit-still capacities around 16,200 litres.
production.maturation: Maturation is managed on site with warehousing capacity for around 20,000 casks; the distillery also operates its own cooperage and bottling plant.

profiles.houseCharacter: Tullibardine combines mineral-rich Ochil Hills water with a straightforward four-pot-still Highland production setup and on-site control from distillation through maturation and bottling. Its stainless-steel fermentation regime is comparatively conventional, placing greater emphasis on clean spirit production and subsequent wood management. The extensive on-site warehousing and cooperage give the distillery unusually direct control over cask handling after distillation.
profiles.cask23Narrative: Tullibardine is a particularly self-contained Highland operation: almost every stage after malting happens on the Blackford site. Danny Burn water feeds a four-still plant, while casks are matured, maintained and eventually bottled within the same distillery complex. That makes wood management and on-site control central to understanding the Tullibardine style.

profiles.location: The Wire Works, Ambergate, Derbyshire, England

production.malt: Wire Works is made as a lightly peated English single malt; White Peak places strong emphasis on local provenance and flavour creation during mashing and fermentation.
production.fermentation: Fresh live brewer's yeast is collected from Thornbridge Brewery. White Peak states that Wire Works uses extended fermentation, with current first-party technical material describing 140-hour fermentations; earlier production writing documents a 96-hour regime, showing deliberate evolution toward longer fermentation.
production.stills: The distillery uses traditional copper pot distillation and double distils its whisky. Exact pot-still capacities are not admitted because they are not published in the verified first-party source set.
production.peat: The house spirit is lightly peated, intended to provide elegant smoke beneath the fermentation-derived fruit rather than dominate the profile.
production.maturation: Wire Works uses a broad wood programme including STR ex-red-wine casks, ex-bourbon barrels, virgin American oak and other wine casks; maturation and bottling take place at White Peak.

profiles.houseCharacter: White Peak deliberately uses fresh live brewer's yeast and very long fermentation to maximise fruit and aromatic complexity before distillation. Light peat adds a restrained smoky layer, while copper pot distillation preserves enough body for active wood influence. STR wine casks, bourbon wood and other oak types then work with rather than replace the fermentation-driven fruit structure.
profiles.cask23Narrative: White Peak is a modern English distillery with a distinctly brewing-led approach to whisky. Fresh Thornbridge brewer's yeast and unusually long fermentation are used to build fruit before the lightly peated wash reaches the copper stills, making fermentation one of the real signatures of Wire Works. The cask programme is broad, but the distillery's own releases repeatedly show that the spirit—not just the wood—is intended to remain visible.

production.waterSource: The distillery sits on a Kentucky River limestone shelf and uses limestone-filtered local water, which naturally removes iron before mashing.
production.malt: Wild Turkey uses non-GMO corn, rye and malted barley across its bourbon and rye mash bills.
production.fermentation: A proprietary yeast strain is used in a sour-mash process. Campari technical material identifies 23 fermenters and an approximately 80-90 hour fermentation, producing a beer around 10% ABV.
production.stills: The main distillation system uses a tall 19-plate column still followed by a doubler/pot-style second distillation. Wild Turkey deliberately distils at a lower proof than the legal maximum to retain more flavour and reduce subsequent dilution.
production.maturation: New make enters new charred American white-oak barrels at a deliberately low proof; the house uses No. 4 char barrels and matures in Kentucky warehouses under the Russell family's long-standing production regime.

profiles.houseCharacter: Wild Turkey combines high-rye grain recipes, a proprietary yeast culture and relatively long sour-mash fermentation to generate a robust, spicy ferment before distillation. The 19-plate column and doubler are operated at deliberately lower proof than the legal ceiling, retaining more congeners and reducing the amount of water needed before barrel entry. Heavy-char American oak then amplifies vanilla, caramel and spice without erasing the grain-driven structure.
profiles.cask23Narrative: Wild Turkey's flavour starts with a production philosophy of keeping more character rather than stripping it away. Limestone water, a proprietary yeast strain and long sour-mash fermentation feed a column-and-doubler system that deliberately distils below the legal maximum proof. The whiskey then enters heavily charred American oak at a relatively low proof, helping explain the dense spice, caramel and grain intensity associated with the house style.

production.waterSource: Water is drawn from the Wolf Burn, rising from a spring near the distillery and naturally filtered through Caithness stone.
production.malt: Wolfburn uses sustainably sourced UK malt and produces both non-peated and lightly peated spirit depending on the production run.
production.fermentation: A single bottom-fermenting yeast strain is used. Wolfburn describes fermentation as deliberately long and unhurried; no exact hour figure is admitted because it is not published in the verified first-party source set.
production.stills: Whisky is double distilled slowly and gently in small copper pot stills. Exact still counts and capacities are not admitted from first-party evidence currently available.
production.peat: The distillery produces both non-peated and lightly peated spirit; official bottling data shows lightly peated examples around 5 ppm, but this is not treated as a universal facility-wide specification.
production.maturation: All whisky is matured on site in traditional-style dunnage warehouses near the sea. Core cask types include first-fill ex-bourbon barrels, first- and second-fill Oloroso sherry butts, rum casks and custom recoopered quarter casks.

profiles.houseCharacter: Wolfburn is built around unhurried production: extended fermentation is followed by slow, gentle small-pot distillation rather than high-throughput spirit stripping. The result is intended to preserve fruit and a smooth, rounded texture before oak influence. On-site dunnage maturation, with bourbon and sherry casks at the centre of the programme, then develops the spirit in Caithness's cool northern climate.
profiles.cask23Narrative: Wolfburn's production philosophy is deliberately patient. Spring water from the Wolf Burn, long fermentation and slow double distillation in small copper stills are all used to create a clean but flavourful spirit before it enters oak. Because every cask matures at the distillery in traditional dunnage warehouses, the northern Caithness environment remains part of the whisky's story from new make to bottle.
